claim: Proteasome-catalyzed peptide splicing (PCPS) of cancer-driving antigens could generate attractive neoepitopes to be targeted by T cell receptor (TCR)-based adoptive T cell therapy.
source: Proteasome-catalyzed peptide splicing (PCPS) of cancer-driving antigens could generate attractive neoepitopes to be targeted by T cell receptor (TCR)-based adoptive T cell therapy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential application of PCPS for generating neoepitopes for therapy.

claim: TCRs were generated against putative KRASG12V- and RAC2P29L-derived neo-splicetopes with high HLA-A*02:01 binding affinity based on a spliced peptide prediction algorithm.
source: Based on a spliced peptide prediction algorithm, TCRs were generated against putative KRASG12V- and RAC2P29L-derived neo-splicetopes with high HLA-A*02:01 binding affinity.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach of generating TCRs based on algorithm predictions.

claim: TCRs generated in mice with a diverse human TCR repertoire specifically recognized the respective target peptides with high efficacy.
source: TCRs generated in mice with a diverse human TCR repertoire specifically recognized the respective target peptides with high efficacy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunization and TCR isolation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The authors failed to detect any neo-splicetope-specific T cell response when testing the in vivo neo-splicetope generation.
source: However, we failed to detect any neo-splicetope-specific T cell response when testing the in vivo neo-splicetope generation and obtained no experimental evidence that the putative KRASG12V- and RAC2P29L-derived neo-splicetopes were naturally processed and presented.
evidence: This is a negative result from experimental testing of in vivo neo-splicetope generation.

claim: Only the putative RAC2P29L-derived neo-splicetope was generated by in vitro PCPS.
source: Furthermore, only the putative RAC2P29L-derived neo-splicetopes was generated by in vitro PCPS.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from in vitro proteasome digestion experiments.

claim: Available algorithms or the in vitro PCPS reaction do not reliably simulate in vivo splicing.
source: The experiments pose severe questions on the notion that available algorithms or the in vitro PCPS reaction reliably simulate in vivo splicing and argue against the general applicability of an algorithm-driven 'reverse immunology' pipeline for the identification of cancer-specific neo-splicetopes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results comparing in vitro and in vivo findings.

claim: Purified 20S proteasomes in combination with synthetic polypeptide substrates reproduced the in vivo generation of epitopes with high fidelity.
source: An important step in defining the proteasome as HLA class I epitope generation machine was the early observation that purified 20S proteasomes in combination with synthetic polypeptide substrates encompassing the epitope of interest reproduced the in vivo generation of these epitopes with high fidelity (Boes et al., 1994; Guillaume et al., 2012; Kessler et al., 2006; Niedermann et al., 1995; van der Bruggen and Van den Eynde, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proteasomes can fuse excised peptide fragments in a reverse proteolysis reaction, generating new immune reactive spliced epitopes (splicetopes).
source: Our view on antigen processing was significantly extended by analysis of cancer patient-derived CD8+ T cells revealing that by proteasome-catalyzed peptide splicing (PCPS) proteasomes can also fuse excised peptide fragments in a reverse proteolysis reaction, thereby generating new immune reactive spliced epitopes (splicetopes) with an amino acid sequence that differs from that of the substrate protein (Hanada et al., 2004; Vigneron et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Splicetope-specific CD8+ T cells derived from tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) inhibited the engraftment of human acute myeloid leukemia cells in SCID mice.
source: The isolation of splicetope-specific CD8+ T cells from cancer patients and the finding that splicetope-specific CD8+ T cells derived from tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) inhibited the engraftment of human acute myeloid leukemia cells in SCID mice indicated the potential immune relevance of such tumor antigen-derived splicetopes (Robbins et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: For FGF-5 and several splicetopes derived from gp100mel, in vitro proteasome splicing reactions mimicked the in vivo splicing reactions.
source: Importantly, for the fibroblast growth factor (FGF)-5 and several splicetopes derived from the tumor differentiation antigen gp100mel, in vitro proteasome splicing reactions were also found to mimic the in vivo splicing reactions (Ebstein et al., 2016; Warren et al., 2006), suggesting that in vitro PCPS reactions may be a useful tool to discover new spliced epitopes generated from tumor antigens of interest.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CD8+ T cells from Listeria monocytogenes–infected mice specifically recognized two phospholipase PlcB-derived splicetopes generated by the proteasome in vitro and in vivo.
source: Testing the feasibility of such an algorithm-aided 'reverse immunology' approach, we had isolated CD8+ T cells from Listeria monocytogenes–infected mice that specifically recognized two phospholipase PlcB-derived splicetopes generated by the proteasome in vitro and in vivo (Platteel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Targeting somatic cancer-specific driver mutations derived from neoantigens by TCR-mediated adoptive T cell transfer (ATT) represents a promising approach for personalized cancer therapy.
source: Targeting somatic cancer-specific driver mutations derived from neoantigens by TCR-mediated adoptive T cell transfer (ATT) represents a promising approach for personalized cancer therapy (Blankenstein et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: KRAS is one of the most frequently mutated genes in human cancer with the G12X substitution accounting for most of the mutations found in this position.
source: KRAS is one of the most frequently mutated genes in human cancer with the G12X (X = V, S, D, A, C) substitution accounting for most of the mutations found in this position.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KRAS mutations in cancer.

claim: None of the KRAS G12X mutations result in the formation of a non-spliced (linear) high-affinity HLA-A*02:01 binding neoepitope (IC50 <100 nM).
source: However, none of these mutations result in the formation of a non-spliced (linear) high-affinity HLA-A*02:01 binding neoepitope (IC50 <100 nM).
evidence: This is an inference based on computational prediction of HLA binding affinity.

claim: KRAS harbors the oncogenic mutation G12V in approximately 30% of pancreatic ductal adeno carcinoma and 20% of the colon and non-small cell lung cancers.
source: Since KRAS harbors the oncogenic mutation G12V in approximately 30% of pancreatic ductal adeno carcinoma and 20% of the colon and non-small cell lung cancers, we used the algorithm ProtAG for theoretical prediction of spliced peptides delineated from the KRASG12V2-35 protein sequence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the frequency of KRAS G12V mutations in specific cancers.

claim: The algorithm-predicted spliced 9mer peptides KRASG12V5-8/10-14 (KLVV/GAVGV, IC50 33.4; sp1), KRASG12V5-9/11-14 (KLVVV/AVGV, IC50 37.50; sp2), and KRASG12V5-10/12-14 (KLVVVG/VGV, IC50 72.90; sp4) have predicted HLA-A*02:01 binding affinity IC50 <100 nM.
source: Using this approach led to the identification of putative nonamer neo-splicetopes (KRASG12V5-8/10-14, KLVV/GAVGV, IC50 33.4; sp1), (KRASG12V5-9/11-14, KLVVV/AVGV, IC50 37.50; sp2), and (KRASG12V5-10/12-14, KLVVVG/VGV, IC50 72.90; sp4), of which sp1 and sp2 allowed for TCR generation (Blankenstein et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction using netMHCpan 4.0 algorithm.

claim: ABabDII mice harbor the human TCRαβ gene loci as a source for a diverse human TCR repertoire that is selected by chimeric HLA-A*02:01.
source: To analyze the immunogenicity of spliced epitopes, we utilized transgenic mice (ABabDII mice) that harbor the human TCRαβ gene loci as a source for a diverse human TCR repertoire that is selected by chimeric HLA-A*02:01 (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research describing the mouse model.

claim: Immunization with the peptides KLVVGAVGV and KLVVVAVGV (representing sp1 and sp2, respectively) induced a CD8+ T cell response in ABabDII mice.
source: Upon immunization with the peptides KLVVGAVGV and KLVVVAVGV (representing sp1 and sp2, respectively), these mice mounted a CD8+ T cell response detected by in vitro re-stimulation of peripheral blood lymphocytes 7 days after the last immunization, whereas mice without immunization did not show reactivity (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: One TCR directed against sp1 epitope (1376) and two TCRs specific for sp2 epitope (9383B2 and 9383B14) were isolated from immunized ABabDII mice.
source: One TCR directed against sp1 epitope (1376) and two TCRs specific for sp2 epitope (9383B2 and 9383B14) were isolated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TCR isolation experiments.

claim: All three TCRs (1376, 9383B2, and 9383B14) induced robust IFNγ release at peptide concentrations of up to 10−10 M, suggesting high functional avidity.
source: All three TCRs induced robust IFNγ release at peptide concentrations of up to 10−10 M, suggesting high functional avidity for these TCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from peptide titration assays shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TCR1376 and TCR9383B2 showed cross-reactivity to the in silico predicted linear KRASG12V KLVVVGAVGV peptide only at the highest peptide concentrations.
source: For TCR1376 and TCR9383B2, cross-reactivity to the in silico predicted linear KRASG12V KLVVVGAVGV peptide was only seen for the highest peptide concentrations (Figure 1D and not shown, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: KRASG12V splice-specific TCRs (1376, 9383B2, and 9383B14) do not recognize cancer cells endogenously expressing mutant KRASG12V.
source: In contrast, IFNγ release by TCR1376 (Figure 2A, B) or TCR9383B2 and TCR9383B14 engineered T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B) was not above background when cancer cells were co-cultured without prior peptide loading, indicating that the endogenous KRASG12V protein is not recognized.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Peptide-loaded cancer cells were recognized by TCR1376, TCR9383B2, and TCR9383B14 transduced T cells.
source: In all cases, peptide-loaded cancer cells were recognized by TCR1376 (Figure 2A, B, red bars) or TCR9383B2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, red bars) and TCR9383B14 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, orange bars) transduced T cells, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pre-treatment of cancer cells with IFNγ 48 hr prior to co-culture did not induce recognition by sp2-specific TCRs.
source: Cancer cells were also treated with IFNγ 48 hr prior to co-culture with the respective TCR-modified PBMCs. As exemplarily shown for sp2-specific TCRs, again only peptide-loaded tumor cells were recognized (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TCR1376-positive T cells efficiently recognized the KRASG12V5-8/10-14 peptide when loaded onto MCF7, Mel624, and mouse NIH-HHD cells or when expressed as a triple epitope.
source: As shown in Figure 3B–D, TCR1376-positive T cells efficiently recognized the KRASG12V5-8/10-14 peptide when loaded either onto MCF7 (Figure 3B), Mel624 (Figure 3C), and mouse NIH-HHD (Figure 3D) cells or when expressed as a triple epitope.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: No IFNγ release was elicited with cells expressing the triple KRASG12V1-35 35mer polypeptide.
source: In contrast, no IFNγ release was elicited with cells expressing the triple KRASG12V1-35 35mer polypeptide (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: KRASG12V triple minigene 35mer is expressed almost twice as high as the KRASG12V triple epitope spliced nonamer.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis of KRASG12V triple minigene 35mer and KRASG12V triple epitope spliced nonamer revealed that KRASG12V triple minigene 35mer is expressed almost twice as high as the KRASG12V triple epitope spliced nonamer (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The spliced peptide KRASG12V5-8/10-14 is either not generated in vivo or is produced at amounts insufficient to be recognized by KRASG12V5-8/10-14-specific high-affinity T cells despite overexpression of the KRASG12V1-35 substrate.
source: Altogether, this indicates that the spliced peptide, theoretically predicted, is either not generated in vivo or, despite the overexpression of the KRASG12V1-35 substrate, is produced at amounts insufficient to be recognized by KRASG12V5-8/10-14-specific high-affinity T cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results with overexpression constructs.

claim: TCR1376 cross-reacts with HLA-C*07 allele.
source: Upon co-culture with a panel of lymphoblastoid B cell lines (BLCLs) that harbor a series of different HLA class I molecules, a test for potential HLA allo-reactivity that we routinely perform with TCRs obtained from ABabDII mice, we uncovered reactivity to several BLCLs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), all of them having in common the expression of HLA-C*07 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: K562-C*07:01 and K562-C*07:02 cell lines were recognized by three independent TCR1376-transduced PBMC donors irrespective of loading with peptide sp1.
source: The experiments showed that K562-C*07:01 and K562-C*07:02 cell lines were recognized by three independent TCR1376-transduced PBMC donors irrespective of loading with peptide sp1, whereas K562-A02:01 cells only induced IFNγ release when these cells were loaded with sp1 peptide prior to co-culture (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TCR1376 directly recognizes members of the HLA-C*07 sub-family and/or peptides bound therein as well as sp1 peptide bound to HLA-A*02:01.
source: These results clearly indicate that the TCR1376 directly recognizes members of the HLA-C*07 sub-family and/or peptides bound therein as well as sp1 peptide bound to HLA-A*02:01.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on HLA cross-reactivity.

claim: Immunization of ABabDII mice with an adenovirus expressing the N-terminal 35mer polypeptide of KRASG12V1-35 as a triple minigene did not induce a CD8+ T cell response to linear or spliced epitopes.
source: Despite multiple immunizations, neither restimulation with the linear 10mer KLVVVGAVGV nor with the spliced epitopes sp1 KLVVGAVGV, sp2 KLVVVAVGV, sp3 YLVVVGAVGV, or sp4 KLVVVGVGV induced IFNγ release by CD8+ T cells in an intracellular cytokine staining of PBMCs 7 days after the last immunization (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The KRASG12V mutation is not immunogenic in the context of HLA-A*02:01, irrespective of whether splicing events occur or not.
source: This supports the notion that the KRASG12V mutation is not immunogenic in the context of HLA-A*02:01, irrespective of whether splicing events occur or not.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative immunization results.

claim: The polypeptide substrates KRASG12V2-35 and KRASG12V2-32 encountered considerable difficulties during synthesis and subsequent purification due to extreme hydrophobicity of the KRAS protein, resulting in a highly impure product not suited for in vitro digestion experiments.
source: However, due to the extreme hydrophobicity of the KRAS protein, the designed longer polypeptide substrates KRASG12V2-35 and KRASG12V2-32 encountered considerable difficulties during synthesis and subsequent purification, resulting in a highly impure product not suited for in vitro digestion experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: All three predicted 9mer KRASG12V spliced peptides (KRASG12V5-8/10-14 sp1, KRASG12V5-9/11-14, sp2, KRASG12V5-10/12-14, sp4) were found to be generated from the KRASG12V2-14 substrate in in vitro PCPS reactions.
source: At t = 0, none of the predicted spliced neo-splicetopes was identified. However, following the generation of the KRASG12V-derived putative spliced neoepitopes from the polypeptide substrates KRASG12V2-14 and KRASG12V2-21 over time in in vitro PCPS reactions (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5), all three predicted 9mer KRASG12V spliced peptides (KRASG12V5-8/10-14 sp1, KRASG12V5-9/11-14, sp2, KRASG12V5-10/12-14, sp4) were found to be generated from the KRASG12V2-14 substrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Using the longer KRASG12V2-21 polypeptide substrate for the in vitro PCPS reactions, only the putative neo-splicetopes KRASG12V5-8/10-14 and KRASG12V5-10/12-14 were generated.
source: Using the longer KRASG12V2-21 polypeptide substrate for the in vitro PCPS reactions, only the putative neo-splicetopes KRASG12V5-8/10-14 and KRASG12V5-10/12-14 were generated (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The accumulation of hydrophobic amino acid residues within the KRASG12V polypeptide substrates led to mistakes during polypeptide synthesis, resulting in the synthesis of faulty polypeptides mimicking in sequence the results of the predicted splicing reaction.
source: Indeed, we found that most likely the accumulation of hydrophobic amino acid residues within the KRASG12V polypeptide substrates had led to mistakes during polypeptide synthesis, resulting in the synthesis of faulty polypeptides (Supplementary file 2) mimicking in sequence the results of the predicted splicing reaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B, Willimsky et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: It was impossible to decide whether the candidate KRASG12V-derived spliced peptides identified in vitro were true splicing products or the product of normal proteasomal cleavage of already preexisting faulty polypeptides.
source: Therefore, it was impossible to decide whether the candidate KRASG12V-derived spliced peptides identified in vitro were true splicing products or as it appeared the product of normal proteasomal cleavage of already preexisting faulty polypeptides inappropriately simulating a splicing event.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the discovery of faulty polypeptides in the substrate.

claim: Using a new KRASG12V1-21 polypeptide substrate without contaminants mimicking the predicted KRASG12V5-8/10-14 (sp1) and KRASG12V5-10/12-14 (sp4) splicing events, the authors failed to identify generation of either predicted KRASG12V 9mer neo-splicetope.
source: We eventually obtained a KRASG12V1-21 polypeptide substrate (JPT Peptide Technologies, Berlin, Germany) without contaminants mimicking the predicted KRASG12V5-8/10-14 (sp1) and KRASG12V5-10/12-14 (sp4) splicing events. However, using this new KRASG12V1-21 polypeptide as substrate for kinetic in vitro PCPS experiments, we now failed to identify generation of either predicted KRASG12V 9mer neo-splicetope.
evidence: This claim is supported by negative results from in vitro PCPS experiments with a clean substrate.

claim: RAC2 is a small GTPase belonging to the Rho family of GTPases.
source: RAC2 is a small GTPase belonging to the Rho family of GTPases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAC2 protein.

claim: The RAC2P29L mutation is a driver mutation facilitating tumor growth as well as metastasis.
source: The RAC2P29L mutation is another so-called driver mutation facilitating tumor growth as well as metastasis and thus presents a potential target in ATT.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RAC2P29L mutation.

claim: The linear RAC2P29L FLGEYIPTV epitope has been predicted with an IC50 of 2 nM.
source: The linear RAC2P29L FLGEYIPTV epitope has been predicted with an IC50 of 2 nM.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction of HLA binding affinity.

claim: The spliced RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 (28FLGEYIP34/36VF37) peptide, with a calculated HLA-A*02:01 binding affinity of IC50 = 24.7 nM, was found to be the only HLA-A*02:01 restricted putative RAC2P29L neo-splicetope with an IC50 < 100 nM generated in in vitro PCPS reactions.
source: In this search, the spliced RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 (28FLGEYIP34/36VF37) peptide, with a calculated HLA-A*02:01 binding affinity of IC50 = 24,7 nM, was found to be the only HLA-A*02:01 restricted putative RAC2P29L neo-splicetope with an IC50 < 100 nM generated.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from in vitro PCPS experiments and computational prediction.

claim: In vitro generation of the non-spliced RAC2P29L28-36 neoepitope was approximately 200-fold more efficient than generation of the putative neo-splicetope RAC2P29L28-34/36-37.
source: However, judging by ion counts in vitro generation of the non-spliced RAC2P29L28-36 neoepitope was approximately 200-fold more efficient than generation of the putative neo-splicetope RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The RAC2P29L28-34/36-40 FLGEYIP/VFDNY polypeptide is the largest already spliced epitope precursor peptide identified in in vitro kinetic experiments.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 4B in in vitro kinetic experiments and by detailed mass spectrometric analyses, we identified the RAC2P29L28-34/36-40 FLGEYIP/VFDNY polypeptide being the largest already spliced epitope precursor peptide.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Generation of the final RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 neo-splicetope requires an additional C-terminal proteasomal cleavage step for spliced epitope liberation.
source: This suggests that generation of the final RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 neo-splicetope requires an additional C-terminal proteasomal cleavage step for spliced epitope liberation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the identification of the precursor peptide and the final product.

claim: No IFNγ release was obtained for the putative neo-splicetope RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 using TCR20967A2-transduced T cells co-cultured with Mel21a cells expressing a triple RAC2P29L1-45 45mer polypeptide minigene.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, no IFNγ release was obtained for the putative neo-splicetope RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 using TCR20967A2-transduced T cells, while peptide-loaded Mel21a cells were readily recognized and IFNγ production demonstrated the target specificity of the TCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Despite the overexpression of the RAC2P29L1-45 45mer substrate peptide, the authors failed to verify the in vivo generation of the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 peptide.
source: Thus, despite the overexpression of the RAC2P29L1-45 45mer substrate peptide, we failed to verify the in vivo generation of the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 peptide.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results with overexpression constructs.

claim: Mel21a cells transduced to express a triple RAC2P29L1-45 45mer or RAC2P29L cDNA were readily recognized by T cells transduced with TCR22894 (linear RAC2P29L-specific TCR).
source: Because Mel21a cells, transduced to express a triple RAC2P29L1-45 45mer (Figure 5B) or RAC2P29L cDNA (Figure 5C), were readily recognized by T cells transduced with TCR22894, we could exclude that our inability to detect cell surface expression of the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 peptide was due to defects in the antigen presentation pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The non-spliced RAC2P29L neoepitope (derived from RAC2P29L1-45 45mer as well as cDNA) was efficiently presented by NIH-HHD cells.
source: As observed in Mel21a cells, the non-spliced RAC2P29L neoepitope (derived from RAC2P29L1-45 45mer as well as cDNA) was efficiently presented also by NIH-HHD cells, excluding potential differences in the catalytic properties of mouse and human proteasomes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The spliced peptide-specific TCR20967A2 did not confer any reactivity to T cells upon co-culture without prior peptide loading of the target cells or overexpression of the spliced epitope.
source: More importantly, again the spliced peptide-specific TCR20967A2 did not confer any reactivity to T cells upon co-culture without prior peptide loading of the target cells or overexpression of the spliced epitope (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: RAC2P29L1-45 45mer polypeptide minigene is expressed almost fivefold higher than the RAC2P29L triple epitope spliced nonamer in mouse NIH-HHD cells.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis of the triple RAC2P29L1-45 45mer polypeptide minigene and RAC2P29L triple epitope spliced nonamer expressed in mouse NIH-HHD cells revealed that RAC2P29L1-45 45mer polypeptide minigene is expressed almost fivefold higher than the RAC2P29L triple epitope spliced nonamer (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Even if the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 neo-splicetope is derived from an overexpressed substrate protein, its amounts are negligible and insufficient to allow its recognition by T cells.
source: However, they clearly demonstrate that even if the RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 neo-splicetope is derived from an overexpressed substrate protein, its amounts are negligible and insufficient to allow its recognition by T cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results with overexpression constructs.

claim: In vitro generation of spliced epitopes by PCPS may not exhibit the same fidelity and does not always simulate the efficacy of in vivo spliced epitope generation.
source: Thus, quite in contrast to the experience resulting from proteasome-dependent processing of non-spliced epitopes in vitro, in vitro generation of spliced epitopes by PCPS may not exhibit the same fidelity and does not always simulate the efficacy of in vivo spliced epitope generation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: In vitro PCPS even when combined with peptide binding and TAP transport assays are not sufficient for the prediction of immune relevance of neo-splicetopes.
source: Reconsidering the workflow for the identification of neo-splicetopes, it thus seems that in vitro PCPS even when combined with peptide binding and TAP transport assays are not sufficient for the prediction of their immune relevance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results.

claim: It is mandatory to first prove the cell surface presentation of algorithm-predicted candidate neo-splicetopes before TCR generation.
source: We therefore believe that it is mandatory to first prove the cell surface presentation of algorithm-predicted candidate neo-splicetopes, either in humanized mice under conditions requiring processing and presentation or by peptide elution experiments, before TCR generation.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' experimental findings.

claim: The frequency of spliced epitopes is largely overestimated.
source: Our data also support the notion (Mylonas et al., 2018) that the frequency of spliced epitopes is largely overestimated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the negative experimental results, supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The amount of cell surface-presented spliced epitope seems to be considerably less than initially estimated.
source: Thus, in light of recent reports (Mylonas et al., 2018; Rolfs et al., 2019) the amount of cell surface-presented spliced epitope seems to be considerably less than initially estimated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: The abundance of spliced epitopes presented at the cell surface is a matter of substantial controversy.
source: Although in these cases the generation efficiency of spliced epitopes in in vitro PCPS assays seemed to be in line with the in vivo situation, it should be noted, however, that the abundance of spliced epitopes presented at the cell surface is a matter of substantial controversy (Liepe et al., 2016; Liepe et al., 2019; Mylonas et al., 2018; Paes et al., 2019; Rolfs et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple papers with differing views.

claim: High-quality peptide synthesis reaches a purity of 95–99% at most.
source: Because high-quality peptide synthesis reaches a purity of 95–99% at most, a thorough substrate analysis appears essential to avoid false-positive results in in vitro PCPS experiments, particularly for chemically difficult substrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptide synthesis quality.

claim: Even minor amounts of faulty peptide substrates will become prevalent in in vitro splicing reactions because the generation of spliced peptides is significantly less efficient than that of non-spliced peptides.
source: Considering that in general the generation of spliced peptides is significantly less efficient than that of non-spliced peptides (Figure 4A), even minor amounts of faulty peptide substrates will become prevalent in in vitro splicing reactions (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on relative generation efficiency.

claim: High substrate and proteasome concentration used for in vitro PCPS may force splicing reactions that do either not or only inefficiently occur under in vivo conditions.
source: One possible explanation for the failure to verify the in vitro PCPS reaction for RAC2P29L28-34/36-37 in in vivo settings could be the high substrate and proteasome concentration as used for in vitro PCPS, thereby forcing splicing reactions that do either not or only inefficiently occur under in vivo conditions where only a single substrate protein enters the catalytic cavity of the proteasome for processing at a given time.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: Epitope generation efficiency of both non-spliced and spliced epitopes is determined by the sequence of the epitope, its surrounding protein sequence, and connected with the cleavage site usage and cleavage strength of proteasomes.
source: In addition to substrate amounts and protein turnover rates, epitope generation efficiency of both non-spliced and spliced epitopes is determined by the sequence of the epitope, its surrounding protein sequence, and connected with the cleavage site usage and cleavage strength of proteasomes (Mishto et al., 2014; Niedermann et al., 1995; Sijts and Kloetzel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Algorithms predicting proteasomal generation of immune-relevant non-spliced epitopes still do not reach prediction efficiencies sufficient for large-scale 'reverse immunology' approaches.
source: However, due to the complexity of protein sequences and lacking information on cleavage strength that decisively determines epitope generation efficiency, algorithms predicting proteasomal generation of immune-relevant non-spliced epitopes still do not reach prediction efficiencies sufficient for large-scale 'reverse immunology' approaches (Calis et al., 2015; Di Carluccio et al., 2018; Singh and Mishra, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Prediction algorithms for spliced epitopes based on protein sequence and proteasomal cleavage properties do not yet exist.
source: Prediction algorithms for spliced epitopes, which are based on protein sequence and proteasomal cleavage properties, do not even yet exist.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: In vitro generation of epitopes using purified 20S proteasomes and synthetic polypeptide substrates in combination with mass spectrometric analyses and both in vitro and in vivo CD8+ T cell assays represents the most frequently used tool to validate the generation of immune-relevant non-spliced peptides.
source: Therefore, in vitro generation of epitopes using purified 20S proteasomes and synthetic polypeptide substrates encompassing the epitope(s) of interest, in combination with mass spectrometric analyses and both in vitro and in vivo CD8+ T cell assays, still represents the most frequently used tool to validate the generation of immune-relevant non-spliced peptides, assuming that it closely simulates the in vivo (in cellulo) situation with respect to both quality and relative amounts of the epitope (Kessler et al., 2001; Kessler and Melief, 2007; Sijts and Kloetzel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing standard methodology.
